\[
a\mid b^2,\qquad b\mid a^2.
\]
Also every proper divisor of \(a\) is a divisor of \(n\) smaller than \(a\), and there are only four divisors of \(n\) below \(a\). Hence
\[
\tau(a)-1\le 4 \implies \tau(a)\le 5.
\]
Thus \(a\) is of one of the forms
\[
p,\quad p^2,\quad p^3,\quad p^4,\quad pq
\]
with primes \(p<q\).

Checking these possibilities using \(a\mid b^2,\ b\mid a^2\) and the fact that \(b\) is the immediate next divisor after \(a\), the prime-power cases are impossible. Hence \(a=pq\).

Then \(b\) must be one of
\[
p^2q,\quad pq^2,\quad p^2q^2.
\]
If \(b=pq^2\), then \(p^2q\) is a divisor between \(a\) and \(b\), contradiction. If \(b=p^2q^2\), then \(p^2q\) is again a divisor between \(a\) and \(b\), contradiction. Therefore
\[
b=p^2q.
\]
Now
\[
n=p^2q^2(1+p^2).
\]
Since \(p^2<a=pq\), it is one extra divisor below \(a\). Also \(1+p^2<a\), so to have exactly one extra divisor below \(a\), we need
\[
1+p^2=q.
\]
This forces \(p=2\), hence \(q=5\). Thus
\[
a=10,\qquad b=20,
\]
and
\[
n=10^2+20^2=500.
\]
Indeed, the divisors of \(500\) begin
\[
1,2,4,5,10,20,\ldots
\]
so \(d_5=10,d_6=20\), and the condition holds.

\[
\boxed{500}
\]
